data.title: Middle East Eye: Tortured into confessing: Report exposes abusive Israeli interrogation of Palestinians
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Tortured into confessing: Report exposes abusive Israeli interrogation of Palestinians
In 2021, Israeli police arrested a Palestinian man known as R, who after multiple rounds of torture, signed a confession document for a crime he did not commit.
He is one of hundreds of Palestinians featured in a report by the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI) who faced criminal proceedings on the basis of confessions extracted under duress.
The man, whose name was withheld for fear of reprisals, spent months in prison before video footage showed he had been nowhere near the scene of the crime he was accused of.
Before that video came to light, R repeatedly tried to withdraw his confession to the unspecified crime but was tortured by Shin Bet officials regardless.

data.title: Middle East Eye: The gold-filled mountains of Chad that hold the key to Libya's crisis and Sudan's war
data.author: MEE correspondent
data.summary:
The gold-filled mountains of Chad that hold the key to Libya's crisis and Sudan's war
Submitted by
MEE correspondent
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 14:23
A mining dispute in a town of a few thousand people tucked away in the remote roof of the Sahara has become entangled with an arms corridor sustaining one of the world’s deadliest wars
The Tibesti mountains run through northern Chad into southern Libya, and are home to the Tubu people (MEE)
Off
Deep inside the Tibesti mountains of northern Chad, in the central Sahara, the town of Miski sits surrounded by a succession of never-ending wadis.
A couple of families live at the top of each of these valleys and in August, when the rainy season comes, the wadis become a river that washes through the mountains. When the rains go, the valleys become green and camels feed on them.
A remote volcanic range characterised by rugged, bare rock, rivers of lava and volcanoes that climb to 3,000 metres, the Tibesti, which runs through northern Chad across the border into southern Libya, is sometimes called the roof of the Sahara.
These mountains are home to the Tubu, an indigenous community whose territory also includes a part of southern Libya, northern Niger and northwestern Sudan.
And the valleys that surround the town of Miski contain vast deposits of a precious metal that throughout human history has been prized almost above anything else: gold.
The mountains, too, are filled with antimony, a toxic heavy metal that is putting the ecosystem of this indigenous community at severe risk and is also exported in great quantities.
For decades, the gold that sits in this remote place has been one of the drivers of armed conflict between the Tubu and the Libyan, then Chadian states.
Now, the Tubu find themselves caught up in a web of warfare and illicit trade that stretches out from Chad into Libya, Sudan and over the sea to the United Arab Emirates, from where arms and supplies are flown to proxy armies, militias and paramilitaries.

data.title: Middle East Eye: US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has undercut US President Donald Trump's assertion earlier this month that he "won't be paying Israel" by the end of this year.
Huckabee, the former governor of Arkansas who is an evangelical pastor and a staunch Zionist - by his own description - said on Tuesday at a conference in Tel Aviv that he's "not certain that there will be a cessation on an abrupt basis by the end of this year".
That's because Washington currently gives Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028.
The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes.

data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Loud explosions rock Riyadh as Houthis attack Saudi ports
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 21:13
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman expected to travel to the US next month for G-20 in first trip since start of war
This aerial photograph shows a view of the Riyadh skyline on 23 November 2026
Off
Fresh explosions rocked Riyadh on Wednesday as Yemen's Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, as the kingdom’s deterrence and defensive capabilities continue to be challenged.
The Houthis said that both strikes on the ports “resulted in damage” while the Saudi-led coalition acknowledged that a projectile hit the port of Jazan, resulting in minor damage and no casualties.
The port strikes followed an attack on Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery. Argus Media, which covers commodity markets, said the Houthis landed two successful blows on the facility, one at the refinery and one at the export terminal. The Houthis say they bombed Ras Tanura as retaliation for the Saudi attack on the port of Hodeidah controlled by the group.
Saudi Arabia is shooting down the majority of Houthi missiles and drones fired at it, Arab and Western officials tell Middle East Eye, but it has failed to protect key assets like energy facilities, financial centres and airports.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has tried to rally the US and regional states to his side. Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey and Syria have all sent or committed to delivering military support to Saudi Arabia, but with the exception of Syria - which has sent drone operators - the assistance is defensive.
The Crown Prince met US Central Command chief admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of forces in the Middle East, last week. MEE first reported the planned meeting, which was the third since fighting with the Houthis resumed in July.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Hezbollah chief demands release of five detained members
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Hezbollah chief demands release of five detained members
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem on Wednesday demanded the immediate release of five men identified as members of the Lebanese movement and accused of forming an armed cell.
Speaking in a televised address broadcast by Hezbollah's Al-Manar channel, Qassem said the men had "done nothing wrong" and "must be released immediately".
Security forces had detained the five earlier this month in a mountainous area in northern Lebanon, a predominantly Christian region far from Hezbollah's main strongholds.
A judge on Wednesday ordered their continued detention pending investigation, a judicial source told AFP.
"We are being patient in order to preserve civil peace, but patience in the face of injustice has limits," Qassem warned, adding the group would "push back against danger" if necessary.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UK moving military planes into hangars amid drone threat: Reports
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
UK moving military planes into hangars amid drone threat: Reports
Britain's air force is moving planes into hangars and hardened shelters overnight to protect them from drone threats, The Times and Sky News reported on Wednesday.
The two UK media outlets also revealed plans by the Royal Air Force (RAF) to install anti-drone nets around warplanes that remain exposed.
The Ministry of Defence did not confirm the reports, but in a statement to AFP said it takes "the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously and (is) always adapting to counter any potential threats".
The ministry said it was "investing an additional £470 million ($615 million) to strengthen security at military sites, including better physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities".
British authorities have regularly issued warnings about the threats posed by Russia and Iran and the government has urged the country to be prepared for different contingencies.
